131: Hill concludes the fertile fields for new leadership, noting the world is undergoing rapid change requiring media adaptation. He then presents 'Media Through Which Services May Be Marketed': (1) EMPLOYMENT AGENCIES—select only reputable agencies with adequate records. (2) ADVERTISING in newspapers, trade journals, and magazines—classified for clerical positions, display for executive connections, with copy prepared by an expert. (3) PERSONAL LETTERS OF APPLICATION—neatly typed, hand-signed, with complete resume of qualifications, prepared by an expert. (4) APPLICATION THROUGH PERSONAL ACQUAINTANCES—particularly advantageous for executive connections. (5) APPLICATION IN PERSON—with a complete written statement of qualifications. He then introduces 'Eight Musts for an Effective Resume': it should be prepared as carefully as a lawyer's court brief. The eight items: (1) Education—briefly state education and specialization with reasons. (2) Experience—describe similar experience fully with former employers' names and addresses.
132: The resume items continue: (3) References—attach photostatic copies of letters from former employers, teachers, and prominent people. (4) Photograph—attach a recent unmounted photograph. (5) Apply for a specific position—never apply for 'just a position,' which indicates lack of specialized qualifications. (6) State qualifications for the particular position—give full details of why you believe you're qualified; this is THE MOST IMPORTANT DETAIL, determining what consideration you receive. (7) Offer to go to work on probation—offer to work a week or month without pay to let the employer judge your value; this indicates confidence in your ability and is most convincing. If accepted and you make good, you'll likely be paid for the probation period. (8) Knowledge of your prospective employer's business—research the business thoroughly and indicate this knowledge in your resume, showing imagination and real interest. Hill notes it's not the lawyer who knows the most law but the one who prepares the best case who wins.
133: Hill advises not to fear making the resume too long—employers want all available information, as their success depends on selecting well-qualified lieutenants. Neatness indicates a painstaking person. He has helped prepare resumes so striking they resulted in employment without personal interview. The resume should be neatly bound and printed, with a cover showing the applicant's name, the position sought, and the company name. It should be on fine paper with a photograph. Successful salespeople groom themselves carefully—first impressions are lasting, and the resume is the sales representative. If the position is worth having, it's worth pursuing with care. Selling yourself impressively may yield more money from the start than applying the usual way. If using an employment agency, ensure they use copies of your resume or produce one meeting all criteria. Hill then introduces 'How to Get the Exact Position You Desire' with seven actions: First, decide and define in writing exactly what job you desire—if it doesn't exist, create it. Second, choose the specific company or individual. Third, study the prospective employer's policies, personnel, and advancement chances. Fourth, analyze yourself to determine what you can offer. Fifth, forget about 'a job'—concentrate on what you can give. Sixth, put your plan on paper with an experienced writer. Seventh, present it to the proper authority—every company wants people who can give value.
134: Hill states this procedure may take days or weeks of extra time but saves years of hard work at small pay, often saving one to five years in reaching a chosen goal. Everyone who starts halfway up the ladder does so by deliberate planning (except the Boss's kid). He then introduces 'THE NEW WAY TO MARKET SERVICES: Jobs Are Now Partnerships.' Men and women must recognize the stupendous change in employer-employee relationships. The 'Golden Rule,' not the 'Rule of Gold,' will dominate. The future relationship will be a partnership of employer, employee, and the public they serve. Both employer and employee will be 'fellow employees' whose business is to SERVE THE PUBLIC EFFICIENTLY. In the past, they bartered among themselves at the public's expense. The real employer of the future is the public. 'HOW TIMES HAVE CHANGED!'—the 'public be damned' policy is passe, supplanted by 'we-are-obligingly-at-your-service, sir.' 'Courtesy' and 'service' are the watchwords, applying to those marketing personal services even more directly than to employers, because both are EMPLOYED BY THE PUBLIC THEY SERVE.
135: Hill shares a personal experience from the Depression: months in Pennsylvania's anthracite coal region studying conditions that all but destroyed the coal industry. He discovered that greed on the part of operators and employees was the chief cause of lost business and jobs. Through pressure of overzealous labor leaders and operators' greed for profits, the anthracite business dwindled. They drove sharp bargains with each other, adding costs to coal prices until they BUILT UP A WONDERFUL BUSINESS FOR OIL BURNING OUTFIT MANUFACTURERS AND CRUDE OIL PRODUCERS. Hill references the Biblical 'Whatsoever a man soweth, that shall he also reap.' The Depression's cause is traceable to the habit of trying to REAP without SOWING. The trouble is that people sowed the wrong seed—service inadequate in quality and quantity, trying to GET WITHOUT GIVING. This principle of cause and effect controls business, finance, transportation, and individuals, determining their economic status. He then introduces 'What Is Your QQS Rating?'—the QUALITY, QUANTITY, and SPIRIT of service determine price and duration of employment.
136: Hill explains the 'QQS Formula': QUALITY plus QUANTITY plus proper SPIRIT equals perfect salesmanship of service. (1) QUALITY means performing every detail in the most efficient manner possible, with greater efficiency always in mind. (2) QUANTITY means the HABIT of rendering all service of which you are capable, increasing as skill develops—emphasis on HABIT. (3) SPIRIT means the HABIT of agreeable, harmonious conduct inducing cooperation. Adequacy of QUALITY and QUANTITY alone is insufficient—the SPIRIT determines both price and duration. Andrew Carnegie stressed this point most, emphasizing HARMONIOUS CONDUCT. He would not retain anyone, regardless of work quality or quantity, unless they worked in a spirit of HARMONY. Carnegie insisted on people being AGREEABLE, permitting conforming individuals to become wealthy while nonconformers had to make room for others. A pleasing personality enables rendering service in the proper SPIRIT—these assets often compensate for deficiencies in QUALITY and QUANTITY. Nothing can substitute for pleasing conduct. Hill then discusses 'The Capital Value of Your Services': the person selling personal services is subject to the same rules as merchants selling goods.
137: Hill states the new way of marketing services has forced employer-employee partnerships considering the public's rights. The 'go-getter' has been supplanted by the 'go-giver.' High-pressure methods blew the lid off, and future business will require no pressure. The capital value of brains can be determined by multiplying annual income by 16.667 (since annual income represents approximately six percent of capital value). Competent brains, if effectively marketed, represent a more desirable capital form than that for goods businesses—brains cannot be depreciated through depressions, stolen, or spent. Money is worthless as a sand dune until mixed with efficient brains. Hill then presents 'THE 30 MAJOR CAUSES OF FAILURE: How Many of These Are Holding You Back?' He notes life's greatest tragedy is people who earnestly try and fail. His analysis of several thousand people showed 98 percent were classed as failures—something is radically wrong with civilization and education. He identifies 30 major failure causes and 13 success principles. Cause (1): UNFAVORABLE HEREDITARY BACKGROUND—the only cause not easily corrected, bridgeable only through the Master Mind. (2): LACK OF A WELL-DEFINED PURPOSE—98 of 100 analyzed had no aim; perhaps the MAJOR CAUSE. (3): LACK OF AMBITION TO AIM ABOVE MEDIOCRITY. (4): INSUFFICIENT EDUCATION—overcome easily; the best-educated are often self-made; education is knowledge effectively and persistently APPLIED. (5): LACK OF SELF-DISCIPLINE—must control self before controlling conditions; self-mastery is the hardest job.
138: The 30 Major Causes of Failure continue: (6) ILL HEALTH—many causes are controllable: overeating non-nutritious foods, wrong thought habits, wrong use of sex, inadequate exercise, improper breathing. (7) UNFAVORABLE ENVIRONMENTAL INFLUENCES DURING CHILDHOOD—'As the twig is bent, so shall the tree grow.' (8) PROCRASTINATION—'Old Man Procrastination' stands within everyone's shadow; most wait for the 'time to be right'; start where you stand with available tools. (9) LACK OF PERSISTENCE—most are good starters but poor finishers; there is no substitute for PERSISTENCE; failure cannot cope with it. (10) NEGATIVE PERSONALITY—success comes through POWER attained via cooperation; negative personality won't induce it. (11) LACK OF CONTROLLED SEXUAL URGE—sex energy is the most powerful stimulus to action and must be controlled through transmutation. (12) UNCONTROLLED DESIRE FOR 'SOMETHING FOR NOTHING'—the gambling instinct drives millions to failure, as seen in the 1929 Wall Street crash. (13) LACK OF A WELL-DEFINED POWER OF DECISION—successful people decide promptly and change slowly; failures decide slowly and change quickly and often. (14) ONE OR MORE OF THE SIX BASIC FEARS—must be mastered before marketing services effectively. (15) WRONG SELECTION OF A MATE IN MARRIAGE—unharmonious marriage destroys ambition and brings misery.
139: The 30 Major Causes continue: (16) OVER-CAUTION—those who take no chances get what's left; over-caution is as bad as under-caution. (17) WRONG SELECTION OF ASSOCIATES IN BUSINESS—we emulate those we associate with; pick an employer worth emulating. (18) SUPERSTITION AND PREJUDICE—superstition is a form of fear and ignorance; successful people keep open minds. (19) WRONG SELECTION OF A VOCATION—no one succeeds in a line they don't like. (20) LACK OF CONCENTRATION OF EFFORT—the jack-of-all-trades is seldom good at any; concentrate on one DEFINITE CHIEF AIM. (21) THE HABIT OF INDISCRIMINATE SPENDING—spendthrifts stand eternally in FEAR OF POVERTY; form the habit of saving 15-20 percent (5 percent minimum) of monthly income; money in the bank gives COURAGE when bargaining. (22) LACK OF ENTHUSIASM—without it one cannot be convincing; enthusiasm is contagious. (23) INTOLERANCE—closed minds seldom get ahead; intolerance means stopped acquiring knowledge. (24) INTEMPERANCE—overindulgence in eating, drink, drugs, or sex is fatal to success. (25) INABILITY TO COOPERATE WITH OTHERS—more people lose positions for this fault than all others combined. (26) POSSESSION OF POWER NOT ACQUIRED THROUGH SELF EFFORT—quick riches are more dangerous than poverty. (27) INTENTIONAL DISHONESTY—no substitute for honesty; those dishonest by choice will pay by loss of reputation or liberty.
140: The 30 Major Causes conclude: (28) EGOTISM AND VANITY—these are red lights warning others to keep away; FATAL TO SUCCESS. (29) GUESSING INSTEAD OF THINKING—most prefer acting on opinions created by guesswork rather than acquiring FACTS. (30) LACK OF CAPITAL—common among first-time business starters without sufficient reserve to absorb mistakes. (31) Name any particular cause not listed. Hill notes this list describes the tragedy of life for those who try and fail. He recommends having someone who knows you well help analyze yourself against these causes, since most cannot see themselves as others see them. 'Know thyself!' is the oldest admonition. You must know your weaknesses to bridge or eliminate them, and your strengths to call attention to them when selling services. He illustrates with a young man who, when asked his salary expectation, had no fixed sum (lack of definite aim), and when told he'd be paid what he was worth after trial, replied he was getting more than that at his current job—an absurd contradiction. Hill warns: before negotiating salary, BE SURE YOU ARE WORTH MORE THAN YOU NOW RECEIVE. Wanting money is different from being WORTH MORE—value is established entirely by ability to render useful service or induce others to render it.
